explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul writes, "Finally, brothers, pray for us…" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). The man has a whole letter's worth of things he could ask for, and he asks for prayer. Plain and simple, and it fits in any pocket.

Good guess, since this is a letter and a reply sounds natural. But Paul never asks for one here. What he writes is "Finally, brothers, pray for us…" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). Prayer is the request, not a reply.

I get it, a team on the road might need a lot of things. But Paul doesn't ask for supplies or money in this verse. He says, "Finally, brothers, pray for us…" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). That's the whole ask.

explanations.answer: It spreads quickly and is honored
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul asks them to pray "that the word of the Lord may spread quickly and be held in honor…" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). Quickly AND honored. He wants it moving fast and treated with respect, like a hot batch that gets eaten with gratitude.

explanations.answer: It stays hidden until the right time
explanations.explanation: Whoa, friend, that's the opposite direction. Paul wants the word of the Lord to "spread quickly" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). Nothing in the verse says to hide it or wait. It's a word on the move.

explanations.answer: It is kept among the church leaders
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody is locking this one in a leaders-only cabinet. Paul prays that the word of the Lord "may spread quickly and be held in honor…" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). Spreading is the whole point, so it's meant to travel.

True! Paul says the word of the Lord should be held in honor, "just as it was with you" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). So the Thessalonians already knew how that looked. He's basically saying, do for others what you already did, and I'm asking God for the same.

Close, but the verse says otherwise. Paul asks that the word of the Lord "may spread quickly and be held in honor, just as it was with you" (2 Thessalonians 3:1). That "just as it was with you" tells us it was already honored among them. They were the example.
Right on, baker. Paul says, "And pray that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men…" (2 Thessalonians 3:2). He asks for rescue from people, not from weather or hunger. Short list, clear request.

I can see why you'd pick it, those are hard things. But Paul doesn't mention either one here. He asks them to pray "that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men…" (2 Thessalonians 3:2). His worry is people.

Plenty of sea trouble shows up in the Bible, but not in this verse. Paul writes, "And pray that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men…" (2 Thessalonians 3:2). No boats in sight, friend, just people.

I see the pull, but look at the end of the verse. Paul says, "…for not everyone holds to the faith." (2 Thessalonians 3:2). That's the opposite of everyone. Some people don't hold to it, and that's part of why he asks for prayer.
That's right! Paul says, "…for not everyone holds to the faith." (2 Thessalonians 3:2). Not everyone. He's honest that some people don't, and he asks for prayer about the wicked and evil men.

explanations.answer: Strengthen and guard them from the evil one
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Paul says, "But the Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one." (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Two things, strengthen and guard. And the one doing it is the Lord, not the believers white-knuckling it alone.

explanations.answer: Take away every trouble in their lives
explanations.explanation: Nice hope, but that's not what the verse promises. Paul says the Lord "will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one." (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Strength and guarding, and nothing there says every trouble disappears.

explanations.answer: Bring Paul back to stay with them
explanations.explanation: Paul does care about them, but he doesn't say that here. The verse reads, "But the Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one." (2 Thessalonians 3:3). The promise is about what the Lord does for them.

That's the one, baker. Paul writes, "And we have confidence in the Lord that you are doing and will continue to do what we command." (2 Thessalonians 3:4). His confidence sits in the Lord. Anybody can say "I believe in you," but Paul puts it somewhere sturdy.

Good thinking, but the word isn't law. Paul says, "And we have confidence in the Lord that you are doing and will continue to do what we command." (2 Thessalonians 3:4). His confidence is in the Lord Himself.

I see why, since leaders come up in churches. But this verse doesn't mention elders at all. Paul says, "And we have confidence in the Lord…" (2 Thessalonians 3:4). The Lord is where his confidence rests.

Not quite, friend. Paul says, "…you are doing and will continue to do what we command." (2 Thessalonians 3:4). "Are doing" means they've already started. He's cheering on something that's already going.
Right! Paul says they "are doing and will continue to do what we command." (2 Thessalonians 3:4). Are doing, so they've begun, and will continue. That's a proud-dad kind of sentence, and I love it.

That's right, baker. Paul writes, "May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance." (2 Thessalonians 3:5). Perseverance means keeping on, which fits believers who are going through hard times. It's the kind of staying power you need in a long bake.

Miracles are a big part of Jesus' story, so I see the guess. But they aren't in this verse. Paul says, "May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance." (2 Thessalonians 3:5).

Wisdom is a fine thing to want, but it isn't the word Paul uses. He writes, "May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance." (2 Thessalonians 3:5). The word is perseverance.

Yes! Paul writes, "May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance." (2 Thessalonians 3:5). Two things in one line, God's love and Christ's perseverance. Both are in the same prayer.

Look again, baker, because it's right there. Paul writes, "May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance." (2 Thessalonians 3:5). God's love is the first thing named, and Christ's perseverance comes right after.
